gapNote: No report ran on 7 July — a one-day gap (last report: 6 July). Significant intervening Iran/Hormuz developments are carried forward in the dominant story summary below. The missed daily report is not backfilled.

global.headline: IRAN — HORMUZ TANKER ATTACKS TRIGGER US STRIKES AND OIL-WAIVER REVOCATION; CEASEFIRE FRACTURES DURING FUNERAL WEEK
summary: On July 7, projectiles and a drone struck three commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the Qatari-flagged LNG carrier Al Rekayyat was hit on its port side near Limah, Oman and caught fire (crew safe), a Saudi-flagged crude tanker was also damaged, and a third vessel was struck by a drone. It was the first attack on shipping in the strait since June 29, reversing the gradual traffic recovery reported in recent weeks. Iranian state television implied Tehran carried out the strike on the LNG tanker "after warnings were ignored" but Iran did not directly claim the attack.

US Central Command responded hours later with what it called "a series of powerful strikes" against Iranian air-defence, coastal-surveillance, surface-to-air-missile and anti-ship-missile sites, drone-launch positions and port facilities near Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island and the port of Sirik, using Air Force and Navy tactical aircraft. Iranian state media reported hits on a commercial pier at Sirik, a fishing pier and civilian fishing vessels at Bandar Abbas, and a telecommunications tower. CENTCOM said the strikes were meant "to impose heavy costs" for attacking shipping "crewed by innocent civilians," calling it a clear ceasefire violation.

The same day, the US Treasury revoked the temporary licence issued in June that had allowed Iran to legally export oil, with any production, delivery or sale to be wound down by July 17. Iran's military headquarters called the US response a "miscalculation" and warned that any further US interference in the strait would be met with a "decisive and swift response." Separately, an Iranian deputy foreign minister hardened Tehran's position on IAEA access, saying it would be "reviewed and decided only within the framework of a final agreement" tied to sanctions relief — a harder line than parliament speaker Ghalibaf's earlier outright denial, but still no access granted.

Shipping trackers reported a sharp drop in transits after the attacks. Kpler had counted 31–43 crossings a day in the July 3–5 period — itself well below the 120–140 vessels a day that transited before the war — and the July 7 attacks pushed traffic down further. Brent crude rose about 2.6% to $72.85 a barrel on the news, though it remains near four-month lows. The escalation lands in the middle of Khamenei's state funeral: ceremonies were held in Qom on July 7, with processions due in Iraq's Najaf and Karbala on July 8 ahead of burial in Mashhad — underscoring that the attacks were not directed by Tehran's civilian leadership during a week when the government's attention is elsewhere.
global.geopolitical: This is the most serious breach of the June 17 MOU since it was signed — roughly 21 of the 60 MOU days have now elapsed with the ceasefire visibly cracking rather than consolidating. Revoking Iran's oil-export waiver removes one of Tehran's few remaining economic incentives to keep Hormuz open, which cuts against the US's own stated goal of stabilising the strait. The timing — hours before NATO's Ankara summit formally endorses language calling on Iran to respect freedom of navigation in Hormuz — hands the alliance an immediate, unwelcome vindication of its own communique. With Mojtaba Khamenei still silent and the funeral consuming Tehran's political bandwidth, the IRGC's freedom to act unilaterally in the strait looks, if anything, wider than before.
global.socioeconomic: Oil's reaction so far is modest — a 2.6% jump, not a return to war-premium pricing — suggesting markets still read this as an escalation within the ceasefire rather than its collapse. But the four major container lines already on Cape of Good Hope routing have no reason to reconsider, and war-risk insurance, which had not meaningfully fallen since the MOU, will likely harden further. For Singapore, the exposure is direct: STB's already-downgraded S$31–32.5B 2026 tourism forecast and the record Q3 electricity tariff (34.78 cents/kWh with GST, confirmed by EMA on 30 June, reflecting April–June gas costs from the conflict) both assumed a durable reopening that this attack calls back into question.

global.headline: NATO ANKARA SUMMIT: LEADERS TO ENDORSE €70B UKRAINE PLEDGE TODAY; ZELENSKYY PRESSES TRUMP FOR PATRIOTS
summary: The 36th NATO Summit's Defence Industry Forum and leaders' sessions opened in Ankara on July 7, with all 32 members present plus non-member invitees Ukraine's Zelenskyy and South Korea's Lee Jae-myung. The pre-agreed draft declaration — reached at ambassador level and due for formal leader endorsement on July 8 — reaffirms Article 5 as "ironclad," pledges €70B (~SGD 107B) in military assistance to Ukraine for 2026 with "at least equivalent" levels for 2027, and describes Russia as a "long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability." On Iran, it repeats the call for Iran to respect freedom of navigation in Hormuz — language that gained unplanned urgency after the day's tanker attacks and US strikes.

Members signed defence-industrial deals worth billions at the forum, including a plan to procure five Northrop Grumman high-altitude, long-endurance uncrewed aircraft and a five-year, $40B commitment to counter-drone capabilities.

On stage at the forum, Zelenskyy renewed Ukraine's case for NATO membership and said he would press Trump for additional Patriot interceptor missiles as Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities intensify. A Zelenskyy-Trump bilateral meeting is scheduled for 2:30pm local time on July 8, on the summit's sidelines.
global.geopolitical: The Iran clause in the declaration was written as boilerplate reassurance; the same-day Hormuz attacks turned it into the most immediately relevant line in the text. Turkey hosting a summit built around collective-defence unity while Hormuz — barely 1,500km from Ankara — reignites is the kind of coincidence that will shape corridor conversations more than the prepared remarks. The €70B Ukraine pledge is real money, but NATO has a track record (Madrid, Vilnius, Washington, The Hague) of the gap between pledge and delivered hardware mattering as much as the headline figure.
global.socioeconomic: The Ukraine commitment and the counter-drone/uncrewed-aircraft deals continue to pull European capital and industrial capacity toward defence production. For Singapore, the summit matters structurally rather than directly: the RSAF's F-35 programme and its ties to the UK and US defence-industrial base, and Singapore's own roughly 3% of GDP defence spending, sit downstream of how the transatlantic industrial base being renegotiated in Ankara is ultimately structured.

global.headline: HAMAS DISSOLVES GAZA GOVERNING BODY, CEDES DAY-TO-DAY RULE TO TECHNOCRATIC COMMITTEE
summary: Hamas announced on July 6 the dissolution of the "Emergency Committee" that has run Gaza's civilian administration, clearing the way for the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) — a body established in January under the US-brokered "Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict" and described as "transitional, technocratic and apolitical" — to take over day-to-day governance. It ends nearly two decades of direct Hamas administrative control over the territory, dating to 2007.

Analysts characterised the move as largely symbolic: it says nothing about Hamas's disarmament, the central condition Israel has set for a lasting peace deal, and Hamas is not dissolving itself as a movement, only its governing apparatus.
global.geopolitical: Ceding administration without disarming lets Hamas claim compliance with the transition plan's civilian-governance requirement while keeping the leverage that matters most to Israel off the table. Whether the NCAG can actually function — collecting revenue, running services, policing — without Hamas's security apparatus underneath it is the real test, and nothing announced July 6 answers it.
global.socioeconomic: A credible civilian handover is the precondition donor states and multilateral lenders have set before releasing Gaza reconstruction financing, so the announcement is a necessary if not sufficient step toward unlocking that capital. For Singapore, the relevance is indirect but real: reconstruction financing of this scale, if it materialises, is the kind of infrastructure and engineering opportunity Singaporean firms have pursued in comparable post-conflict rebuilds.

global.headline: SUPER TYPHOON BAVI: ROTA DAMAGE ASSESSED AS "EVERY ASPECT" OF THE ISLAND HIT; STORM NOW BEARS DOWN ON TAIWAN
summary: Full damage assessments from Rota, the US Pacific island hit directly by Super Typhoon Bavi on July 6, describe damage to "every aspect" of the island — most homes damaged or destroyed, the airport and seaport both damaged, and the island's roughly 2,000 residents without power or running water. No fatalities have been reported on Rota or across the wider Northern Marianas and Guam, where tens of thousands remain without power but most structures held up.
Bavi has since continued west-northwest and is now forecast to bring life-threatening conditions and gusts near 200mph to Taiwan.
global.geopolitical: Zero confirmed fatalities despite Category 5-equivalent force is a genuine mitigating outcome and will shape how the US federal disaster-response effort on Rota, a CNMI territory, is judged politically. Taiwan bracing for the same storm system adds a fresh dimension given the island's outsized strategic weight — any disruption to Taiwan's infrastructure lands in a far more geopolitically sensitive context than a 2,000-person Pacific island.
global.socioeconomic: Rota's rebuild — homes, utilities, port and airport — falls almost entirely on US federal emergency appropriations. Taiwan is the more consequential economic exposure: it is Singapore's largest single trading partner (~US$134B in bilateral trade in 2025, MTI, semiconductor-driven), so any storm-related disruption to Taiwanese fabs or ports is a direct, if likely short-lived, risk to Singapore-linked supply chains.

singapore.headline: MHA TABLES ROAD TRAFFIC BILL: HANDHELD-PHONE BAN, LOWER DRINK-DRIVE LIMITS, TOUGHER DANGEROUS-DRIVING TERMS
summary: The Ministry of Home Affairs tabled the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill for first reading in Parliament on July 7. It makes it an offence to hold a mobile communication device — phone, tablet or wearable — in hand while a vehicle is moving, regardless of whether it is actually being used, removing the current need to prove usage. First-time offenders face a fine of up to S$1,000 and/or up to 6 months' jail; repeat offenders face up to S$2,000 and/or 12 months. Devices mounted on a holder remain permitted.

The Bill also lowers the prescribed alcohol limits — the breath-test limit from 35 to 15 micrograms per 100ml, and the blood limit from 80 to 30 milligrams per 100ml — bringing Singapore in line with Taiwan, Japan and South Korea, and raises the maximum jail term for first-time dangerous driving causing grievous hurt from 5 to 7 years.
MHA cited a worsening road-safety trend as the rationale: traffic fatality rates rose about 24% and traffic violations about 38% between 2021 and 2025.
singapore.geopolitical: The alignment with East Asian peer limits on drink-driving is a deliberate regional benchmarking move, positioning Singapore's road-safety regime alongside jurisdictions it typically compares itself to on regulatory rigour rather than against looser Western thresholds.
singapore.socioeconomic: Removing the need to prove phone usage makes the handheld offence far easier to enforce and prosecute, which should raise both compliance costs for delivery and ride-hailing fleets and fine revenue. Lower alcohol limits will also affect the food and beverage and nightlife sectors' liability exposure and could dent late-night ride-hailing demand at the margin.

singapore.headline: PARLIAMENT: NO FURTHER ACTION ON WP'S SYLVIA LIM, FAISAL MANAP OVER COMMITTEE OF PRIVILEGES FINDINGS — TIME BAR
summary: Leader of the House Indranee Rajah delivered a ministerial statement on July 7 confirming that Parliament will take no further action against Workers' Party MPs Sylvia Lim and Faisal Manap over the Committee of Privileges' findings arising from the Raeesah Khan lying-under-oath case. The conduct occurred during the 14th Parliament, and under Section 22 of the Parliamentary (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act, the 15th Parliament — convened after the 2025 General Election — has no power to impose penalties for conduct in a dissolved Parliament.
Indranee noted the House could still pass a motion of regret if it wished, but is not obliged to.
singapore.geopolitical: The episode is a reminder that parliamentary accountability mechanisms in Singapore's system reset at dissolution, closing off sanction for conduct once a general election intervenes — a structural point that will likely resurface in future privileges cases regardless of which party is involved.
singapore.socioeconomic: Limited direct economic bearing; the main consequence is political rather than financial, closing out a carryover matter from the previous term without further formal censure of the two WP MPs.

word.definition: The breaking out again, often more virulently, of something (a disease, conflict, or bad situation) that had been dormant or in remission.
word.etymology: From Latin recrudescere, "to become raw again" — from re- ("again") + crudescere, an inceptive verb formed from crudus ("raw, bleeding"). Originally a strictly medical term for the return of symptoms after apparent healing, extended into general and political usage by the 19th century.
word.example: Tuesday's tanker attacks and the US strikes that followed are a recrudescence of the Hormuz conflict just as it had begun, tentatively, to heal — the wound reopening in the same place, during the very week Iran was meant to be burying the man under whom it was first inflicted.
